title: 😰 Google and Microsoft's AI stress test
body_text: One of the hardest parts of life behind bars is going years without your favorite comfort meal. I mean, who would want to go a day without eating Vegemite, the sticky, dark brown tar-like substance made out of leftover brewer’s yeast? Australians, who often enjoy it smeared in a thin layer over white bread, love it so much one man convicted of murder argued it ought to be a human right for him to enjoy some in prison. Unfortunately, the country’s Supreme Court disagreed, upholding one state’s ban of the product in prisons. One of the reasons it’s banned, prison officials argue, is because it could impair sniffer dogs trained to find drugs and alcohol. Alphabet , the parent company of search giant Google, and Microsoft will report earnings today as investors are increasingly seeking data over vibes to reassure them about the continued health of the AI boom. Both companies are expected to report enormous increases in AI-related spending, raising a familiar question: When will all this investment pay off? And here is what the Street is expecting from Microsoft. $46.5 billion in capital expenditures, up 140% from $19.3 billion during the same period last year. $90.6 billion in revenue, up 16.7% from $77.6 billion during the same period last year. $4.71 earnings per share, up 14% from $4.13 last year. And here is what the Street is expecting for Alphabet: $55.2 billion in capital expenditures, up 130% from $23.9 billion during the same period last year. $127.9 billion in revenue, up 25% from $102.3 billion during the same period last year. $3.03 earnings per share, up 5.6% from $2.87 last year. Meta reported results last week and was punished after reporting negative free cash flow and outlining plans to continue spending aggressively on AI. Increasingly, the worry for companies betting big on AI is that they are taking on debt to fund a product that has not quite proven to be lucrative. But not all AI spending is created equal. Meta, importantly, doesn’t have a cloud business (yet). Its AI investments are largely aimed at improving its existing products, particularly its massive advertising business, while developing new AI-powered services. Google and Microsoft, on the other hand, may be spending a ton on AI but they’re also collecting checks from other companies who are also spending a ton on AI. That’s because they, along with Amazon have compute to sell other AI giants. And those deals represent commitments from big AI players to spend figures that can run into the hundreds of billions going forward. A huge amount of power in the AI industry is in cloud giants like Alphabet and Microsoft. These same cloud companies are also investors in, customers of, and suppliers to major AI model developers. Google and Microsoft can justify their enormous spending plans perhaps more than others: They don't necessarily need to build the next killer AI app to make money. They can sell the computing power to whoever does. title: 🐜 $ANT Man
body_text: A campaign is pushing the New York Public Library to return the set of toys that inspired A.A. Milne to write the Winnie-the-Pooh stories to the United Kingdom once and for all. The NYPL owns the actual Pooh, Piglet, Eeyore, Tigger and Kanga, and a cohort of British fans want them returned to commemorate the 100th anniversary. The United Kingdom attempting to get an institution to return an important cultural artifact to its nation of origin? Well, see now I’ve heard everything. Stocks finished up on Monday, led by tech. Yesterday we wrote that the week ahead would be investors’ quarterly check-in on the AI trade. We didn’t know how right we’d be: on Monday, Anthropic filed for its IPO . A couple interesting things pop out that are relevant to companies posting earnings this week, first and foremost the unique arrangement between Anthropic and three cloud service providers (CSPs): Amazon , Alphabet and Microsoft . Sales through the cloud marketplaces of that trio of companies constituted 48% of Anthropic revenue in H1 of this year, up from 11% in 2023. That’s a bit of a double-edge sword; the willingness of the CSPs to shill Claude to their customers has been a significant driver of revenue growth for Anthropic over the period. On the other hand, this means that half the revenue from Anthropic’s customers aren’t actually from Anthropic’ s customers, they’re from Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft’s customers, and you can be certain that those three firms would love nothing more than to swoop in with their own models if the situation were to present itself. But don’t just take our word for it! It’s right there in the prospectus as a risk, “customers may develop their own solutions that compete with our models, platform, and applications.” It’s complicated, and Anthropic isn’t trying to hide that: “Our relationships with our strategic partners — whether with CSPs, who simultaneously serve as our investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors, or with Broadcom , which simultaneously serves as a supplier and lessor — create potential conflicts of interest that are difficult to fully anticipate or mitigate.” Essentially, not only is it complicated, but given how complicated it is we don’t even know how complicated it’s going to end up being. That hasn’t even touched on the unique ownership structure. As a Public Benefit Corporation, Anthropic has not only the founder supervote that’s become common lately, but also a few other tiers of shareholding with various rights and profit participation: Class T shares, for “humanity,” controlled by a long-term benefit trust that appoints four directors who are there to ensure that Anthropic advances the common good. Neat? Class F shares, for the founders, who get the other three board seats. Class E shares, for employees, which have no economic rights but get to break ties. Class A shares. This means you! The economic rights, your slice of the pie. You get a vote, but one that will always be outvoted by the founders anyway. Class N shares, which is Class A stock with no vote, the shares given to Amazon and Google . The next two weeks will be an investor roadshow for the company, and the IPO date is expected to target the week before Thanksgiving under the ticker symbol ANT on Nasdaq. Expectations for the company vary between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion valuation . Compared to the SpaceX prospectus and the kind of language coming out of OpenAI, the document is relatively sober, even if it does contain risk factors like: “Our most capable models have demonstrated, and future models are expected to demonstrate, capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons.” “More broadly, the long-term effects of regular AI interaction on mental health, cognitive development, and social behavior are not yet fully understood, and if such long-term harms do materialize in the future, we could face significant liability, reputational harm, and adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” “Our proprietary model weights, corporate and financial data, and other core intellectual property represent particularly high-value targets for state-sponsored espionage and theft, and security researchers have identified frontier AI companies as priority targets for non-U.S. intelligence services.” Will that make investors skittish? title: 👾 The AI trade’s quarterly checkup
body_text: New York City had an electric summer following the Knicks victory in the NBA Finals, and that sweet victory was enjoyed by basically everyone, with a few exceptions. One of those exceptions is “people who work for New York Knicks owner James Dolan.” When and how you have heard about the eccentric billionaire cable heir depends on which incredibly weird or petty thing Dolan did that made its way into your feed, from siccing facial recognition technology on perceived adversaries to making his vanity project band, JD & The Straight Shot, the de facto opening act for major stars playing at Madison Square Garden. Still, a new report from The Athletic may take the cake for Dolan lore, as evidently when employees of the Knicks had been eagerly awaiting details on their eligibility for sought-after NBA Champions rings, Dolan insisted that IT send out a phishing test email purporting to offer everyone in the organization a free ring, with the people who clicked on the included link getting not a Knicks ‘26 ring but instead a mandatory cyber-security seminar. The nice thing about business news is that it’s essentially the only category where the subjects legally have to be honest with you at least four times per year (or half that often in Europe). This week we’ll get a look past the bluster, the boasting, the rumors, and the suspicions about what’s actually happening with the AI trade, with companies representing the entire AI behemoth snout-to-tail reporting earnings. The big three are the hyperscalers, the companies that have existing cloud operations and ambitions to supplement those with large AI capital investments: Alphabet , Amazon , and Microsoft . Yes, all of them have their ancillary business that could be megacorps in their own right — Microsoft with its Office and video game divisions (and don’t forget LinkedIn!), Alphabet with its advertising and phone business, and Amazon with its retail operation — but realistically investors are going to be paying attention to their AI buildout, how much it’s costing, the manner in which they intend to cover those costs, and so on. Those costs are other companies’ sales, and we’ll be hearing a lot from them, too. If you want to build an AI data center (and these guys really, really do!) you’ve got to spend money that eventually ends up in the pockets of the disk storage companies ( Sandisk and Seagate are both reporting), the chip manufacturers ( Intel on Thursday, AMD the following week) and the companies that make optical communications equipment ( Corning , on Tuesday) and power and cooling racks ( Vertiv, on Wednesday). Those are just the direct suppliers, but you’ve got to build the things too, and for that you need power generation ( GE Vernova reports Wednesday) and the equipment to construct the things ( Caterpillar , the day after) The long and short of it is that this week will be a check-up on virtually every component of the most important trade in markets. Traders will be making inferences based on these flagship companies for not just the rest of earnings season and their competitors, but also the overall health of the trade itself. The AI trade in general and semiconductors in particular have been rattled for the past few weeks, as my colleague Luke Kawa wrote in EntryPoint last Friday. The VanEck Semiconductor index has taken a beating over the past several months, with semis nearing a dip below the 200 day moving average that could spell algorithm-inflected pain for bulls. This week, we’ll get some serious clarity on what the current state of play is, and even better some insight into where these hyperscalers are forecasting things will go; earnings estimates over the next 12 months for the big guys have plateaued, and it’ll be interesting to see if they happen to agree. “At its core, Netflix dominated the streaming landscape in the early 2020s when other entertainment companies were just entering the streaming landscape.
